newsitem.title: USA: Strong U.S. job growth fans fears of inflation.
newsitem.headline: Strong U.S. job growth fans fears of inflation.

text.p: Job growth was unexpectedly strong in December though the unemployment rate held steady at 5.3 percent, the government said Friday, in a report that reignited inflation jitters on Wall Street.
Stocks fell sharply after the report, though they later recovered, as bond prices tumbled on worries that the Federal Reserve would have to boost interest rates soon in a bid to ward off inflation.
The Labour Department said the economy created 262,000 jobs in December after a revised gain of 127,000 in November. The jobless rate was unchanged from November's revised 5.3 percent.
Economists surveyed by Reuters had pegged December's unemployment rate at 5.3 percent. But they had forecast that only 192,000 new jobs were created.
The report followed a string of data that have pointed to an economy that was strengthening at the end of 1996.
The bond market tumbled on the news since inflation erodes returns on long-term investments like bonds.
The 30-year Treasury bond slid 1-1/2 points, or $15 on a $1,000 bond, pushing its yield up to 6.87 percent from 6.75 percent on Thursday. Bond prices and yields move in the opposite direction.
The Dow Jones industrial average, which fell as much as 67 points after the report, had reversed course and moved higher by midday. It stood at 6,638.37, up 12.70 points, in afternoon trading.
President Clinton said the report provided "further evidence that our economy is strong" and noted inflation pressures that normally occur with such a healthy job market appeared to be absent.
Outgoing Labour Secretary Robert Reich also said wages continued rising at the end of last year without any signs of inflation.
"America has never seen a Goldilocks economic recovery like this. Not too hot. Not too cold. Just right," said Reich, who is leaving the Clinton administration this week.
Reich said brisk growth in jobs in the service and retail sectors defied "the gloom and doomers who warned that increasing the minimum wage would destroy jobs."

For all of 1996, the economy created 2.6 million new jobs outside the farm sector, up from 2.2 million in 1995, the department said in its report. The jobless rate averaged 5.4 percent, compared to 5.6 percent in 1995 and 6.1 percent in 1994, department officials said.

Average hourly earnings rose 6 cents to $12.05 last month after rising 9 cents in November. Those figures irked Wall Street investors who watch them closely since wage inflation can push up consumer prices.

But some economists said they expected the Fed to leave rates unchanged when its policy-makers meet early next month. The central bank has has held short-term rates steady since cutting them to spur economic growth last January.
"The economy's been percolating away but hasn't gone to boil yet. It's not enough to turn the heat up on the Fed to tighten," said Joel Naroff, chief bank economist at First Union.
So far, the economy has absorbed growing demand for labour without producing a runup in inflation, Naroff added.
The report may still heighten concern at the Fed, particularly if further reports continue pointing to robust growth, economists said.

"The risks are a little bit higher that the Fed will have to move (to raise rates) but I don't see them moving in early February," said Tim O'Neill, chief economist at Chicago-based Harris Bank/Bank of Montreal.
The December report showed that the average workweek lengthened to 34.8 hours from 34.5 hours in November.
Factory overtime rose to 4.7 hours from 4.5 in November, while the work week stood at 42.0 hours vs. 41.7. The work week and overtime hours in December stood at their highest levels since early 1995.
Manufacturing added 19,000 jobs in December after no change in November. Despite gains late in the year, 94,000 factory jobs were lost for all of 1996.

The construction industry added 23,000 jobs for the second consecutive month in December, bolstered by milder-than-normal weather across the country, the department said. Retail jobs grew by 48,000, up from 32,000 in November.
Service industry employment rose by 222,000 after growing a revised 103,000 in November.
